headline: The 30-year Treasury yield closed at its highest level since 2007 and Brent crude held above $91 overnight after the US-Iran ceasefire lapsed — while the New York Fed's factory survey hit a four-year high, contradicting Friday's weak consumer data.
stance: The story moved to the far end of the yield curve. The 30-year Treasury yield rose about 3 basis points on Monday to 5.29%, the highest since 2007 and within striking distance of that year's 5.44% peak. What makes it awkward is the direction of the rest of the curve: the 30-year is up about 13 basis points this month while the 2-year is down about 12. Investors are not demanding more to lend for thirty years because they expect a stronger economy — they are demanding more because of the size of the government's borrowing, the volume of long-dated bonds being sold into the market, corporate borrowing for artificial-intelligence projects, and inflation that has run above the Fed's 2% target for five years, at 3.4% in the year to last month. Last week's $25 billion 30-year auction cleared at 5.216%, the highest since 2001, with dealers forced to absorb more than usual. The bond market's own expected-swings gauge jumped to 75.6 from 69.6. Then Monday's data went the other way: the New York Fed's August factory survey came in at 20.6 against 15.6 in July and roughly 11 expected — its strongest in more than four years, three days after retail sales fell 0.6%. Stocks gave up more ground, the S&P 500 falling 0.52% to 7,745.06, and overnight the temporary US-Iran ceasefire lapsed with Brent above $91.

news.head: The 30-year Treasury yield closed at its highest since 2007
news.body: The yield on the 30-year Treasury bond rose about 3 basis points on Monday to 5.29%, a level last seen in 2007, when the peak was 5.44%. The move is concentrated at the long end: the 30-year is up roughly 13 basis points so far this month while the 2-year is down about 12. Four reasons are being cited for it — the scale of government borrowing, the volume of long-dated bonds being sold, heavy corporate borrowing to fund artificial-intelligence projects, and inflation that has sat above the Federal Reserve's 2% target for five years, running at 3.4% over the past twelve months. Barclays' Anshul Pradhan argued that reversing it would take 'some combination of a downside fiscal surprise, slower AI-related issuance, a shift in Treasury's issuance strategy, and a sustained run of soft activity data' — in other words, more than one thing going right.

news.head: Last week's 30-year auction had already shown the strain
news.body: The Treasury sold $25 billion of 30-year bonds last week at a clearing yield of 5.216%, the highest cost on a 30-year sale since 2001. Two details underneath that number matter more than the headline. Bids covered the amount on offer 2.39 times, and the primary dealers — the banks obliged to bid whatever else happens — were left holding 11.5% of the issue. Both figures were below their twelve-month averages, and the awarded yield came in above where the market was trading beforehand. That combination is the standard signature of an auction that had to be dragged over the line rather than one that was met.

news.head: New York factory activity jumped to a four-year high
news.body: The Federal Reserve Bank of New York's August survey of manufacturers, published Monday, put its headline general business conditions index at 20.6 against 15.6 in July and roughly 11.0 expected — its strongest reading in more than four years. The detail is less uniform than the headline: new orders slipped to 17.3 from 22.2 and shipments to 11.7 from 24.4, while unfilled orders were 15.5 and the employment measure 9.3 from 11.4. Costs are the sore point — prices paid rose to 58.6 from 52.3 while prices received fell to 22.7 from 27.6, meaning factories are absorbing the difference. Manufacturers' expectations for six months ahead improved to 32.1 from 27.9.

news.head: The temporary US-Iran ceasefire lapsed and oil went above $91
news.body: Washington ruled out extending the 60-day temporary ceasefire with Tehran, and a senior Iranian official said the country would adopt a 'fully offensive' military posture if diplomacy fails. Brent crude was $91.14 a barrel at about 10:40pm ET Monday, up 27 cents on the session and its highest since July 30, and was still $91.27 at about 2:20am ET Tuesday. Back-channel discussions are reported to be continuing. The last full session reading before that had Brent at $88.52 on August 14.

news.head: Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has nearly stopped
news.body: Five commodity-carrying vessels crossed the Strait of Hormuz on Saturday, against 31 over the previous weekend. That is the physical fact underneath the price: the waterway is not merely disputed in negotiations, traffic through it has largely ceased. Yemen's Houthi forces separately attacked Saudi military vessels and their escorts in the Red Sea, which puts pressure on the second of the two chokepoints at the same time. A shipping route that stays shut turns a geopolitical headline into a supply problem, and a supply problem is what shows up in the inflation figures three months later.

news.head: Stocks slipped again and protection got dearer
news.body: The S&P 500 fell 0.52% to 7,745.06 on Monday, the Nasdaq 100 0.32% to 26,644.91 and the Dow 0.51% to 53,459.78. The VIX — the market's price for insurance against S&P 500 swings over the coming month — closed at 15.19 from 14.25 on Friday, its Nasdaq-100 counterpart at 21.51 from 20.72, and the skew index, which measures what investors pay specifically for protection against a large fall, at 142.9 from 138.4. Three-month insurance was still dearer than one-month, at 19.04, so this is a market paying up for cover in the near term rather than one repricing the whole year.

news.head: Monday's single-stock moves were about memory chips and the used-car consumer
news.body: Carvana fell 7.28%, the worst performer in the S&P 500 on the day, in the same week four large retailers report on what households are actually spending. SanDisk rose 8.88% on strength across memory chipmakers, and Meta Platforms fell 3.54%. Those three in one session describe the split that has run through this market all month: anything tied to the artificial-intelligence build-out is bid, anything tied to a household balance sheet is not.

news.head: Overnight: futures lower with the first of the big retailers reporting today
news.body: At about 2:20am ET, S&P 500 futures were down 0.41%, Nasdaq 100 futures 0.76%, Dow futures 0.16% and Russell 2000 futures 0.24%. The dollar index closed Monday at 99.58 against 99.64 on Friday. Home Depot is scheduled to report second-quarter results before today's opening bell and Baidu also reports today; Target and Lowe's are scheduled for Wednesday and Walmart for Thursday, and the minutes of the Fed's July meeting are published Wednesday.

implications: The bond market and the growth data swapped sides overnight from Friday, and the 30-year is the one to watch. On Friday, weak retail sales and weak sentiment sat alongside rising yields, and oil was the bridge. On Monday the growth data was strong — a four-year high in New York factory activity — and yields rose again, but at the long end rather than across the curve. A 30-year yield rising 13 basis points this month while the 2-year falls 12 is not a growth signal or a Fed signal. It is a price for lending money to the government for thirty years, and it is going up for reasons a rate decision in September cannot fix.

The auction detail is the part worth carrying forward. A 5.216% clearing yield on a 30-year sale is the highest since 2001, but the bid-to-cover of 2.39 and the 11.5% left with primary dealers are what tell you the level was set by a shortage of buyers rather than a change of view. Dealers taking down an above-average share means the market cleared at a concession. If the same pattern shows up at the next long-dated sale, the phrase to use is not 'yields are high' but 'the buyer base has thinned' — and that is a slower, more structural problem than an inflation scare.

Monday's factory survey makes the September argument harder, not easier. A headline at 20.6 against 15.6 removes the cleanest version of the case for holding — that activity is rolling over — three days after retail sales fell 0.6%. But the components do not confirm the headline: new orders and shipments both fell, and prices paid rose to 58.6 while prices received fell to 22.7, which is a margin squeeze rather than a boom. The honest reading is that manufacturing is holding up while the consumer wobbles, and that the Fed is being handed one more month of data that points both ways.

Oil above $91 with the strait effectively shut changes the character of the inflation problem. Five vessels through Hormuz on Saturday against 31 the weekend before is not a risk premium — it is an interruption already happening. That matters more than the price itself, because a premium unwinds when talks resume and an interruption has to be replaced with physical barrels from somewhere else. The 10-year breakeven — the annual inflation rate bond prices imply over the next decade — was 2.28% on Monday's close against 2.27% Friday, so the bond market has priced almost none of this yet.

Corporate credit is still refusing to react, and it is now refusing to react to its own story. The extra yield high-yield bonds pay over investment-grade narrowed to 267 basis points in Friday's reading from 271 on Thursday, with investment-grade at 80. Borrowing to fund artificial-intelligence projects was named among the reasons long-dated government yields rose — yet the market that actually holds that corporate debt tightened. When the government bond market prices a company's borrowing before the corporate bond market does, the two are not both right.

watch.head: Housing starts and import prices at 8:30am ET, industrial production at 9:15am
watch.body: Housing starts and building permits for July land at 8:30am ET alongside import prices, with industrial production and capacity utilisation following at 9:15am. Housing is the part of the economy wired directly to the long end of the curve, and the long end just closed at its highest since 2007 — a 30-year mortgage is priced off that part of the curve, not off the Fed's overnight rate. Import prices are the first read on whether an oil price above $91 and a shut shipping lane are already entering the cost base.

watch.head: Home Depot reports before today's opening bell
watch.body: The first of four large retailers scheduled to report this week, and the results are not out at the time of writing. What the company reports on is the same demand the official retail sales figure said fell 0.6% in July — but from its own receipts rather than a survey estimate, and with the added job of describing what a long-term borrowing rate at a nineteen-year high is doing to the home-improvement chain. Baidu also reports today; Target and Lowe's follow Wednesday, Walmart Thursday.

watch.head: The minutes of the Fed's July meeting, Wednesday
watch.body: The record of the meeting that set the current 3.50%-3.75% target range, published into a market that has moved a long way since. The useful content is the dispersion — how many participants wanted to move in July and what the argument against was — not the conclusion. It was written before the July payrolls contraction, before Friday's retail sales and sentiment figures, and before Monday's factory survey and long-bond selloff, so it dates the committee's thinking rather than forecasting it.

watch.head: Whether the long end keeps going without the rest of the curve
watch.body: The single number to follow this week. A 30-year yield at 5.29% while the 2-year falls is a market repricing the cost of long-term government borrowing rather than the path of policy — and it is happening while the inflation compensation built into 10-year bonds has barely moved, at 2.28%. If the 30-year keeps climbing and breakevens stay where they are, the message is about debt supply and buyer appetite. If breakevens start following oil upward instead, it becomes an inflation story, and the September argument changes shape again.

sections.title: Macro & Rates
bullets: The biggest change since yesterday morning sits at the far end of the curve. The 30-year Treasury yield rose about 3 basis points on Monday to 5.29%, its highest since 2007, when the peak was 5.44%. It is up roughly 13 basis points this month while the 2-year is down about 12 — a steepening driven by the price of long-term government borrowing, not by the outlook for the Fed.

Last week's $25 billion 30-year sale cleared at 5.216%, the highest on a 30-year auction since 2001. Bids covered the amount on offer 2.39 times and primary dealers were left with 11.5% of the issue, both below their twelve-month averages, and the awarded yield came in above where the market had been trading. The level was set by thin demand rather than by a change of view.

The reasons cited are structural rather than cyclical: the scale of government borrowing, the volume of long-dated bonds coming to market, corporate borrowing to fund artificial-intelligence projects, and inflation that has run above the Fed's 2% target for five years — 3.4% over the last twelve months. Barclays' Anshul Pradhan put the conditions for a reversal as a downside fiscal surprise, slower AI-related issuance, a change in how the Treasury issues, and a sustained run of soft activity data.

The rest of the curve moved less. The 10-year yield closed Monday at 4.72% from 4.68% Friday and the 2-year at 4.19% from 4.17%, widening the gap between them to +53 basis points from +51. The 10-year breakeven rose to 2.28% from 2.27% and the inflation-adjusted 10-year yield to 2.44% from 2.41%. Expected swings in Treasury prices jumped to 75.6 from 69.6 — a jump of nearly 9% in a single session.

Monday's data cut against Friday's. The New York Fed's August factory survey came in at 20.6 from 15.6 in July, against roughly 11.0 expected and its strongest in more than four years. Underneath, new orders fell to 17.3 from 22.2 and shipments to 11.7 from 24.4, prices paid rose to 58.6 from 52.3 while prices received fell to 22.7 from 27.6, and expectations for six months ahead improved to 32.1 from 27.9. Strong headline, softer engine, worse margins.

Overnight: Washington ruled out extending the temporary ceasefire with Tehran and a senior Iranian official said the country would take a 'fully offensive' posture if diplomacy fails. Brent crude was $91.14 at about 10:40pm ET, its highest since July 30, and $91.27 by about 2:20am ET, against $88.52 in the August 14 reading. Five commodity vessels crossed the Strait of Hormuz on Saturday against 31 the previous weekend. The dollar index closed at 99.58 from 99.64.
sections.positioning: Every positioning extreme in the rates book sits at the short and middle of the curve, and none of it is where the selling is. In the weekly futures data for positions held through August 11, speculators' net position in 2-year Treasury futures stands at the 98th percentile of the past three years — an extended long, and standing background rather than news, having sat there three weeks — with the 5-year at the 93rd. Nothing is flagged as stretched in the long bond at all. That is the useful part: a 30-year yield making a nineteen-year high without a positioning extreme behind it cannot be explained away as a squeeze on one extended trade. There is no crowd to squeeze — there is simply less demand.

sections.title: Equity Markets
bullets: Monday's close: the S&P 500 fell 0.52% to 7,745.06, the Nasdaq 100 0.32% to 26,644.91 and the Dow 0.51% to 53,459.78 — a second consecutive decline after the index set a record last Thursday.

Insurance repriced across the board. The VIX, the price of protection against S&P 500 swings over the coming month, closed at 15.19 from 14.25 on Friday; its Nasdaq-100 counterpart at 21.51 from 20.72; and the skew index — what investors pay specifically for cover against a large fall — at 142.9 from 138.4. Three-month protection was still dearer at 19.04, so the market is paying up for the next few weeks rather than repricing the year.

Carvana fell 7.28%, the worst performer in the index, in the week four large retailers report on household spending. SanDisk rose 8.88% alongside strength in memory chipmakers and Meta Platforms fell 3.54%. The dividing line remains the artificial-intelligence build-out on one side and the household balance sheet on the other.

The valuation backdrop against which the long end is moving: the cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings ratio for the S&P 500 stood at 42.35 on Monday's close. Company profits are worth more the lower the long-term interest rate used to discount them, and that rate just closed at its highest since 2007.
Overnight, futures pointed lower: S&P 500 down 0.41%, Nasdaq 100 down 0.76%, Dow down 0.16% and Russell 2000 down 0.24% at about 2:20am ET, with Home Depot scheduled before the opening bell.
sections.positioning: The new development in the weekly futures data is in volatility itself. Speculators' net position in VIX futures has dropped to the 10th percentile of the past three years, a fall of 12 percentile points in a single week — an extended short, new this week, with the commercial hedgers who take the other side at the opposite extreme. Read straight, that is a contrarian warning: the speculative money is positioned for calm, into a week that carries the Fed minutes, four large retailers reporting on the consumer, a lapsed ceasefire and a long-bond selloff. Being short volatility is a trade that pays a little most days and costs a great deal on the few that go wrong.

single_name.note: (Liberty Latin America, the cable and mobile operator) — the highest-scoring name on the screen and in its second session on the list. An insider purchase was filed on August 13, the shares trade above their 200-day trend line, and both the scan's dark-pool and options signals are live. It would take under a day and a half of average volume to close out the shares currently sold short, at a borrowing cost of about 0.3% a year — so there is essentially no bearish position to squeeze here. Any move would have to come from the buying itself.

sections.title: Credit & Liquidity
bullets: Corporate credit is now ignoring its own story. The extra yield high-yield bonds pay over investment-grade narrowed to 267 basis points in Friday's reading from 271 on Thursday, with investment-grade spreads at 80 from 79. Borrowing to fund artificial-intelligence projects is being named as one of the forces pushing long-dated government yields to a nineteen-year high — and the market that holds that corporate debt tightened in the same week.

Short-term funding stayed easy, with a small wobble. The spread on commercial paper — the short-term IOUs large companies issue to cover payroll and inventory — stood at 19 basis points in Friday's reading, and the two key bank-funding spreads both sat at minus 1 basis point. The Fed's overnight parking facility held $0.3 billion on Monday against $0.2 billion Friday; there is effectively nothing left in it to cushion a shock.

The reserve picture is unchanged and stays that way until Thursday. The Treasury's own account at the Fed stood at $964.0 billion in last Wednesday's weekly snapshot and bank reserves at $2,944.1 billion, with the Fed's balance sheet 1.75% larger than a year ago. Reserves draining while funding costs stay near zero spread is the benign version of that combination, and it is still the one on the screen.

Broad conditions remain easier than average: the two national financial-conditions gauges were -0.58 and -0.77 in the readings for the week to August 7, where negative means easier than normal. Stocks and corporate credit continue to move together more than usual, with the correlation between them at 0.67. Easy financial conditions and a 5.29% thirty-year yield are not a contradiction — they are what happens when the strain is in government borrowing rather than in private borrowing.
sections.positioning: Credit remains the only one of the five markets tracked with no positioning extreme flagged anywhere in it, while rates, equities, currencies and commodities each carry at least one three-year extreme. That is background rather than news — the weekly figures are unchanged from Friday's publication — but it is the control worth holding onto this week. If the retailers disappoint, the Fed minutes read hawkish and spreads still do not move, then the worry visible in equities and in the long bond is not shared by the people who actually lend to companies.
